Server clocks drift because they rely on physical timing hardware — typically quartz crystal oscillators — whose oscillation frequency varies slightly with temperature, aging, manufacturing tolerances, and supply voltage, causing the clock to run a little fast or slow relative to true time. Those small per-second errors accumulate into seconds, minutes, or more of skew over weeks unless corrected, and other effects like interrupt handling delays, virtualization, suspension, and leap-second handling can add further offsets. To counter this, servers synchronize with external time sources using NTP or its successors (chrony, systemd-timesyncd, PTP for tighter precision), which continuously measure and gently correct the local clock so the whole fleet stays within milliseconds of a common reference.
